44817: Tiberius succeeds Augustus. Luke dates John the Baptist's ministry to the fifteenth year of his reign.
44819: Pilate governs Judea (26–36). A dedicatory stone found at Caesarea Maritima in 1961 names him "prefect of Judea."
44823: In Tiberius's fifteenth year (AD 28/29) John calls Israel to a baptism of repentance in the Jordan.
44828: Jesus, about thirty, is baptized by John; the Spirit descends and the Father speaks. He is then tested forty days in the wilderness.
44832: At a wedding in Cana Jesus turns water into wine, "the first of his signs," and his disciples believe.
44836: On a hill near the Sea of Galilee Jesus teaches the beatitudes, the Lord's Prayer, and the call to a righteousness exceeding that of the scribes.
44840: At Caesarea Philippi Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ; Jesus begins to teach that he must suffer, die and rise.
44842: On a high mountain (traditionally Tabor, possibly Hermon) Jesus is transfigured and speaks with Moses and Elijah about his departure.
44844: Jesus raises Lazarus four days dead; the Sanhedrin, led by Caiaphas, resolves that one man should die for the people.
44846: Jesus rides a colt into Jerusalem amid shouts of "Hosanna," then clears the temple of traders.
44850: Betrayed in Gethsemane, tried before the high priest and Pilate, Jesus is crucified at Golgotha on a Friday at Passover and buried in Joseph of Arimathea's tomb. Astronomical calendars allow Nisan 14 on a Friday in AD 30 or AD 33; both have strong defenders.
44852: On the third day the tomb is found empty; the risen Jesus appears to Mary Magdalene, the women, Peter, the Emmaus travelers, the Eleven and more than five hundred.
44854: After forty days of appearances Jesus commissions the disciples to be witnesses to the end of the earth and is taken up from the Mount of Olives.
44856: The Spirit comes on the disciples with wind and tongues of fire; Peter preaches and about three thousand are baptized. Christians date the church's public beginning here.
44860: Stephen, one of the Seven, is stoned after his speech to the council; Saul approves, and persecution scatters the church.
44861: Philip in Samaria; the Ethiopian official
44862: Philip proclaims Christ in Samaria and on the Gaza road baptizes a court official of the Ethiopian queen.
44866: On the road to Damascus the risen Jesus appears to Saul the persecutor; he is baptized by Ananias and begins proclaiming Jesus as Son of God.
44868: After a vision at Joppa, Peter preaches to the Roman centurion Cornelius; the Spirit falls on Gentiles and they are baptized.
44870: Scattered believers preach to Greeks in Antioch; Barnabas fetches Saul from Tarsus, and the disciples are first called Christians.
44872: Herod Agrippa I beheads James and imprisons Peter, who is freed by an angel; Agrippa dies at Caesarea in AD 44 (confirmed by Josephus).
44875: Sent out from Antioch, Barnabas and Saul cross Cyprus and plant churches in southern Galatia.
44879: Paul defends justification by faith apart from works of the law. On the South Galatian view it is his earliest letter (before the council); on the North Galatian view it dates to the mid-50s.
44881: Apostles and elders decide Gentile believers need not be circumcised, asking them to avoid a few practices offensive to Jewish believers.
44883: Claudius expels Jews from Rome; Suetonius mentions disturbances "at the instigation of Chrestus," often taken as a garbled reference to Christ. Priscilla and Aquila move to Corinth.
44884: Paul's second journey; gospel to Europe
44885: Paul's Macedonian vision brings the gospel into Europe: Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea, Athens and eighteen months in Corinth.
44887: Gallio, proconsul of Achaia, dismisses charges against Paul. The Delphi inscription dates Gallio's term to AD 51–52, the firmest anchor in Pauline chronology.
44889: Paul teaches for over two years in the hall of Tyrannus; the riot of the silversmiths follows. He writes 1 Corinthians here.
44891: From Corinth Paul writes his fullest exposition of the gospel to the church at Rome, carried by Phoebe of Cenchreae.
44893: A temple riot leads to Paul's arrest; he is held two years at Caesarea under Felix, then appeals to Caesar before Festus.
44894: Paul under house arrest in Rome
44895: After shipwreck on Malta, Paul spends two years in Rome proclaiming the kingdom "with all boldness and without hindrance."
44896: James the brother of Jesus killed
44897: Josephus (Antiquities 20.200) records that the high priest Ananus had "James, the brother of Jesus who was called Christ" stoned during an interval between governors.
44899: After the fire of Rome Nero blames the Christians and executes many (Tacitus, Annals 15.44).
44900: Peter and Paul martyred in Rome
44903: Early tradition (1 Clement 5; later Eusebius) holds that Peter was crucified and Paul beheaded in Rome under Nero.
44905: Judea rises against Rome; Vespasian and then Titus campaign through Galilee to Jerusalem. Eusebius reports Jerusalem's Christians fled to Pella.
44907: Titus's legions burn the temple in August AD 70, ending sacrifice; the Arch of Titus in Rome shows the menorah carried in triumph. Jesus had foretold that not one stone would be left on another.
44911: The last rebel stronghold above the Dead Sea falls to Rome (73 or 74).
44915: Exiled on Patmos, John receives visions addressed to seven churches of Asia. Irenaeus places this late in Domitian's reign; some argue for a date under Nero before AD 70.
44919: The church at Rome writes to Corinth urging the restoration of deposed presbyters; one of the earliest Christian writings outside the New Testament.
44921: Tradition (Irenaeus) says John lived in Ephesus into Trajan's reign, the last of the apostles.
44925: Bishop Ignatius is taken to Rome to die in the arena, writing seven letters on the way that stress the bishop, the Eucharist and the real humanity of Christ.
44927: Simon bar Kosiba, hailed by Rabbi Akiva as messiah, leads a second revolt (132–135). Hadrian crushes it, refounds Jerusalem as Aelia Capitolina and bars Jews from the city. Jewish Christians who refused to follow him suffered for it.
44931: The aged bishop of Smyrna, a link to the apostle John, is burned; the Martyrdom of Polycarp is the earliest martyr account outside the New Testament.
44933: The philosopher-apologist Justin, who described Sunday worship and defended Christianity to the emperor, is beheaded in Rome.
44935: Christians in Lyon and Vienne, including the slave girl Blandina, die in the arena; a letter describing them survives in Eusebius.
44936: Bishop of Lyon and hearer of Polycarp, Irenaeus answers Gnosticism with apostolic succession, the rule of faith, the fourfold gospel and recapitulation in Christ.
44938: Decius requires everyone to sacrifice to the gods and obtain a certificate; many lapse, and controversy over their readmission divides Carthage and Rome (Cyprian, Novatian).
44940: Edicts order churches destroyed, scriptures burned and clergy arrested; it is the most severe empire-wide persecution.
44942: Constantine and Licinius grant freedom of worship to Christians and restore confiscated property, a year after Constantine's victory at the Milvian Bridge.
44943: The first ecumenical council rejects Arius and confesses the Son "of one substance" (homoousios) with the Father; it also sets a common rule for dating Easter.
44945: Constantine refounds Byzantium as his new capital, the center of Christian empire in the east for over a thousand years.
44946: Athanasius's Easter letter lists the NT canon
44947: Athanasius's 39th Festal Letter lists exactly the twenty-seven books of the New Testament as canonical.
44949: The second ecumenical council affirms the full deity of the Holy Spirit and expands the Nicene Creed into the form still recited, building on the Cappadocian Fathers.
44950: In a Milan garden Augustine hears "take up and read," reads Romans 13 and turns to Christ; later bishop of Hippo, he shapes Western theology of grace, sin and the church.
44951: Working in Bethlehem, Jerome translates the Old Testament from Hebrew and revises the Latin gospels; the Vulgate becomes the Western church's Bible.
44953: Alaric's Visigoths sack Rome; in response Augustine writes *The City of God*.
44955: The third ecumenical council rejects Nestorius and affirms Mary as Theotokos ("God-bearer"), insisting Christ is one person.
44957: The fourth ecumenical council defines Christ as one person "in two natures, without confusion, change, division or separation." Oriental Orthodox churches reject the formula, causing a lasting division.
44958: End of the western Roman Empire
44959: Odoacer deposes the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus; the eastern (Byzantine) empire continues from Constantinople.
44960: Convened by Justinian, the fifth ecumenical council condemns the "Three Chapters" and reaffirms Chalcedon in a Cyril-friendly key; it is also associated with the condemnation of Origenist teachings.
44962: Gregory organizes famine relief, sends missionaries to England (596) and writes pastoral works that shape medieval ministry.
44964: Muhammad's migration (hijra) from Mecca to Medina begins the Islamic calendar; within a century Arab armies conquer the Levant, Egypt, North Africa and Persia.
44968: Patriarch Sophronius surrenders Jerusalem to Caliph Umar; Christians become a protected minority under Islamic rule.
44971: Caliph Abd al-Malik completes the Dome of the Rock on the Temple Mount.
44972: The seventh ecumenical council ends the first phase of iconoclasm, distinguishing veneration of icons from worship due to God alone.
44974: Pope Leo III crowns Charlemagne on Christmas Day, reviving a western empire and deepening the estrangement from Constantinople.
44976: Papal legates excommunicate Patriarch Michael Cerularius, who excommunicates them in return. Disputes over papal authority, the filioque and unleavened bread had built for centuries; the break hardened after 1204.
44977: Anselm of Canterbury argues that sin dishonors God and only a God-man can render the satisfaction owed, a landmark in atonement theology.
44979: Western crusaders capture Jerusalem with great slaughter and found the Latin kingdoms; the crusades poison relations with Muslims, Jews and Eastern Christians.
44981: Latin crusaders sack the Christian capital of the East, hardening the schism.
44982: Innocent III's council defines transubstantiation and requires annual confession and communion.
44984: Thomas Aquinas synthesizes Aristotelian philosophy and Christian doctrine (1265–1274), defining scholastic theology.
44985: John Wycliffe and associates translate the Vulgate into English; his followers, the Lollards, are suppressed.
44987: The Czech reformer, condemned by the Council of Constance despite a safe-conduct, is burned; the Hussite movement endures.
44989: Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II takes the city, ending the Byzantine Empire; Hagia Sophia becomes a mosque.
44990: Movable-type printing at Mainz produces the Latin Bible, making later Reformation pamphlets and vernacular Bibles possible.
44992: Erasmus publishes the first printed Greek New Testament with a fresh Latin translation; Luther and Tyndale translate from it.
44994: On 31 October Martin Luther circulates theses against the sale of indulgences in Wittenberg, sparking the Reformation.
44995: Before Emperor Charles V Luther refuses to recant unless convinced by scripture and plain reason; he is outlawed and hidden at the Wartburg, where he translates the New Testament.
44997: In Zurich, Conrad Grebel baptizes George Blaurock, rejecting infant baptism; the Swiss Brethren's Schleitheim Confession follows in 1527.
44998: William Tyndale's New Testament, translated from Greek, is smuggled into England; he is executed in 1536, but much of his wording passes into the King James Version.
45000: Philip Melanchthon's statement of Lutheran faith is presented to Charles V.
45002: John Calvin publishes the first edition of the *Institutes of the Christian Religion* and soon begins his work in Geneva.
45003: The Catholic Church (1545–1563) answers the Reformers on scripture and tradition, justification and the sacraments, and launches internal reform.
45005: A warm Reformed catechism opening with "What is your only comfort in life and death?"
45006: The Authorized Version is published in England and becomes the dominant English Bible for three centuries.
45007: The Dutch Reformed synod (1618–1619) rejects the Remonstrant (Arminian) articles and issues the Canons of Dort, later summarized as the "five points of Calvinism."
45008: The Westminster Assembly completes a confession and catechisms that become standards for Presbyterians worldwide.
45009: Hearing Luther's preface to Romans read in London, John Wesley feels his heart "strangely warmed"; Methodism's field preaching follows.
45011: George Whitefield's tours and Jonathan Edwards's preaching bring revival across the American colonies.
45013: After *An Enquiry* (1792) and the founding of the Baptist Missionary Society, Carey goes to India, opening the modern Protestant missionary era.
45014: Darby and the Brethren shape dispensationalism
45015: John Nelson Darby teaches a distinct future for Israel and a pretribulational rapture of the church in the 1830s, spreading through the Plymouth Brethren and later prophecy conferences.
45017: Constantin von Tischendorf finds leaves of a fourth-century Greek Bible at St. Catherine's Monastery, Sinai (more in 1859), transforming New Testament textual study.
45019: William J. Seymour leads an interracial revival in Los Angeles marked by speaking in tongues; it launches global Pentecostalism.
45020: C. I. Scofield's annotated KJV popularizes dispensational premillennialism among English-speaking evangelicals.
45022: The World Missionary Conference aims at evangelizing the world and seeds the modern ecumenical movement.
45024: The Confessing Church, with Karl Barth as main drafter, rejects Nazi claims over the church: Jesus Christ is the one Word of God.
45026: Bedouin find scrolls in caves near Qumran, including a complete Isaiah scroll a thousand years older than previously known Hebrew manuscripts.
45027: Israel declares independence; the event becomes central in dispensational and Christian Zionist readings of prophecy and is contested by other interpreters.
45028: The Catholic Church (1962–1965) renews liturgy in vernacular languages, encourages Bible reading and opens dialogue with other Christians.
45029: Billy Graham and John Stott convene evangelicals from 150 nations; the Lausanne Covenant joins evangelism and social responsibility.
45031: By about 2000 most Christians live in Africa, Latin America and Asia, with Pentecostal and charismatic forms growing fastest.
45032: The present: the church spans every continent, and Christians await the return of Christ while differing on the order of last things.
